Department of Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology, University of Applied Sciences Darmstadt Darmstadt Germany ([ROR:047wbd030](https://ror.org/047wbd030)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract We designed novel pre-drug compounds that transform into an active form that covalently modifies particular His residue in the active site, a difficult task to achieve, and applied to carbonic anhydrase (CAIX), a transmembrane protein, highly overexpressed in hypoxic solid tumors, important for cancer cell survival and proliferation because it acidifies tumor microenvironment helping invasion and metastases processes. The designed compounds have several functionalities: (1) primary sulfonamide group recognizing carbonic anhydrases (CA), (2) high-affinity moieties specifically recognizing CAIX among all CA isozymes, and (3) forming a covalent bond with the His64 residue. Such targeted covalent compounds possess both high initial affinity and selectivity for the disease target protein followed by complete irreversible inactivation of the protein via covalent modification. Our designed prodrug candidates bearing moderately active pre-vinylsulfone esters or weakly active carbamates optimized for mild covalent modification activity to avoid toxic non-specific modifications and selectively target CAIX. The lead inhibitors reached 2 pM affinity, the highest among known CAIX inhibitors. The strategy could be used for any disease drug target protein bearing a His residue in the vicinity of the active site. ## Introduction Covalently binding compounds performing targeted covalent inhibition (TCI) (Bauer, 2015; Gillette et al., 1974; De Vita, 2021; Singh, 2022) bear special functional groups called ‘warheads’, usually Michael acceptors. Initially, these compounds bind to the target protein reversibly via their specific structural features that recognize the target protein (Lonsdale and Ward, 2018). In a subsequent step, an irreversible covalent bond is formed between the ‘warhead’ fragment and the targeted amino acid, mostly a nucleophilic one like cysteine (Lonsdale and Ward, 2018). This irreversible mode of binding provides a prolonged mechanism of action, full and reversible or irreversibletarget inactivation, the need for lower drug dosages, the opportunity for higher selectivity toward the target, and in some cases – effective inhibition of drug-resistant enzyme mutants (Lonsdale and Ward, 2018; Singh et al., 2012; Sutanto et al., 2020). Among successfully applied targeted covalent inhibition examples are ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor), afatinib (EFGR T790M mutant inhibitor), osimertinib (improved EFGR T790M mutant inhibitor), and sotorasib (KRAS G12C mutant inhibitor), which are already approved by the Food and Drug Administration (Boike et al., 2022; Baillie, 2016). Here, we introduce pre-vinylsulfone warhead for TCI by the formation of a covalent bond with the protein histidine residue. In contrast to cysteine, the intrinsic nucleophilicity of histidine is weaker and there are few reports about histidine labeling in proteins by small molecules, most of them being highly reactive and therefore not usable as warhead in drug development due to non-specific reactions (Jia et al., 2019; McCowen et al., 1951; Harlow and Switzer, 1990; Gilbert et al., 2023). Known histidine-targeting compounds mostly carry a highly reactive warhead, such as sulfonylfluorides, which provide some degree of selectivity due to suitable substituents, which interact selectively with their target protein (Che and Jones, 2022; Cruite et al., 2022), but it is almost impossible to prevent non-specific labeling. Chemoselective modification of histidine is very difficult to achieve. A light-promoted and radical-mediated selective C-H-alkylation of histidine for peptide synthesis has been suggested (Chen et al., 2019), but does not apply to proteins. Another method for chemoselective histidine bioconjugation uses thiophosphorodichloridate reagents, which mimic naturally occurring histidine phosphorylation (Jia et al., 2019). A light-driven selective approach for labeling histidine residues in native biological systems was developed with thioacetal as thionium precursor (Wan et al., 2022). However, the light-driven approach requires the presence of high concentrations of Rose Bengal as a catalyst, not suitable for therapeutic applications. We applied the TCI strategy to human carbonic anhydrases (CA), metalloenzymes that catalyze reversible CO2 hydration by producing acid proton and bicarbonate anion. There are 12 catalytically active CA isozymes in humans. The CAI, II, III, VII, and XIII are cytosolic, CAIV is membrane-bound, while CAVA and VB are found in mitochondria. CAVI is the only secreted isozyme found in saliva and milk, whereas CAIX, XII, and XIV are transmembrane proteins bearing extracellular catalytic domains (Aggarwal et al., 2013). Catalytic domains of CA isozymes are highly homologous and bear structurally very similar beta-fold. However, the isozymes differ in their enzymatic activity, tissue distribution, and cellular localization. CAIX is a hypoxia-inducible protein, which participates in cancer cell proliferation and metastasis (Saarnio et al., 1998; Rafajová et al., 2004). As recently demonstrated by proteomic analysis, CAIX interacts with amino acid and bicarbonate transporters to control cancer cell adhesion, a critical process involved in migration and invasion. The CAIX also plays an important role in the migration of cancer cells by interaction with collagen-, laminin-binding integrins, and MMP-14 (Swayampakula et al., 2017; McDonald et al., 2018). It is proposed that targeting CAIX catalytic activity and/or interrupting the interactions with metabolic transport proteins and cell adhesion/migration/invasion proteins will have therapeutic benefits by involving pH regulation, metabolism, invasion, and metastasis (McDonald et al., 2018; Becker and Deitmer, 2021). Sulfonamides stand out as the most extensively researched class of CA inhibitors (Krishnamurthy et al., 2008; Linkuvienė et al., 2018). They exhibit a high binding affinity in their deprotonated state to the zinc-bound water form of CA (Kovalevsky et al., 2018; Aggarwal et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 1970). Drugs used in the clinic as CA inhibitors, such as acetazolamide, methazolamide, dichlorophenamide, dorzolamide, and brinzolamide, have various side effects (Swenson, 2014). The development of isozyme-selective CA inhibitors is a major goal of drug discovery. Any such drugs will be more beneficial than the currently available mostly non-selective CA inhibitors, as the reduction of side effects will improve the effectiveness of the therapy. Covalent inhibitors have been previously designed for CAI and CAII, namely, bromoacetazolamide and N-bromoacetylacetazolamide (Kandel et al., 1968; Kandel et al., 1970; Cybulsky et al., 1973). Although N-bromoacetylacetazolamide formed a covalent bond with CAI His67 and bromoacetazolamide with CAII His64 amino acids, further research of these compounds was discontinued (Cybulsky et al., 1973). Recently, studies involving covalent modification of CA isozymes (mainly CAII) have been published. However, the synthesized molecules were designed not to act as enzyme inhibitors, but as a model protein to investigate benzenesulfonamide-bearing fluorescent label and a warhead able to bind the enzyme covalently (Swenson, 2014). One of their new probes bearing an epoxide reactive group was not only able to form a covalent bond with the protein, but it did it selectively for His64 (Chen et al., 2003). Similarly, analogous sulfonamides without fluorescent groups were synthesized and formed the covalent bonds with His3 or His4 of CAII (Takaoka et al., 2006; Wakabayashi et al., 2008). Different warheads were applied to react with His64 and His3 (Gilbert et al., 2023; Aatkar et al., 2023) bearing S(IV) fluoride to present a new way for the expansion of the liganded proteome (Gilbert et al., 2023; Aatkar et al., 2023). In this work, we investigated fluorinated benzenesulfonamide compounds bearing sulfonylethyl ester and sulfonylethyl carbamate moieties as possible covalent CA inhibitors. The 3-substituted-2-((2,5,6-tetrafluoro-4-sulfamoylphenyl)sulfonyl)ethyl acetate exhibited a surprisingly high binding affinity for CAIX, which was more than tenfold higher than our previous synthesized lead compound VD11-4-2 (Kd(CAIX)=32 pM) (Dudutienė et al., 2014). The MS and X-ray crystallography data confirmed the covalent binding of new compounds to the proton shuttle His64 residue. We showed that sulfonylethyl ester/carbamate behaves as a prodrug by reacting with His64 in the active site of CAs through the elimination mechanism to release ester or carbamate moieties, thus forming a reactive vinylsulfone group. The newly discovered mechanism of inhibition of CA through forming a covalent bond between the compound and the protein has great potential for developing high-affinity compounds for a particular CA isozyme, and such compounds could become precursors of new-generation drugs. ## Results ### Design and mechanism of covalently-binding CA inhibitors In search of high-affinity and high-selectivity inhibitors of CAs, a series of fluoro-benzenesulfonamide-based compounds were synthesized (Figure 1). The benzenesulfonamide group is important for making a coordination bond with the Zn(II). At the same time, the fluorine atoms were included to withdraw electrons from the sulfonamide group and diminish its pKa to strengthen interaction. Surprisingly, part of the compounds exhibited extremely strong binding affinity. These compounds contained the -SO2CH2CH2OCOR group that was forming an unexpected covalent bond with the protein. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101401/elife-101401-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** Compounds on the left of the vertical dashed line do not form the covalent bond, while the ones on the right form the covalent bond with the protein molecule. Moieties shown in red are important for structural comparison to visualize the chemical groups that are responsible for covalent interaction, high affinity, or high selectivity for CAIX. It has been known in organic chemistry that compounds bearing this fragment in the presence of bases can rearrange to vinyl-sulfonyl moiety which has been reported as a covalently modifying ‘warhead’ (Tsutsui et al., 1987; Alonso et al., 2003; Ichikawa et al., 1989). To the best of our knowledge, this kind of rearrangement/elimination has not been applied to enzyme covalent inhibitors. We designed benzenesulfonamides with the SO2CH2CH2OCOR group that can form highly reactive electrophilic species without adding additional base by adding multiple fluorine atoms to the benzene ring. Furthermore, the rearrangement occurred only in the CA enzyme active site. The active vinyl-sulfonyl group formed via elimination reaction, which occurred easily due to the strong electron-withdrawing effect of fluorines on the benzene ring (Figure 2). ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101401/elife-101401-fig2-v1.jpg) The SO2 group at the para position relative to the sulfonamide group was also necessary for a covalent bond because compounds 4 and 5 bearing the SO or S groups, respectively, did not form the covalent bond with CA isozymes. Moreover, the change of the -O-CO-R group to -NH-CO-R or -CO-O-R also prevented the formation of the covalent bond as illustrated by compounds 2, 10, 7, and 8 that did not form covalent bonds with the protein molecule. We propose the mechanism where the covalent modification occurs via the elimination mechanism shown in Figure 2, where a basic amino acid residue removes the proton and forms the vinylsulfone moiety, which only then forms a covalent bond with the nitrogen atom of the histidine residue. To check this mechanism, two control compounds, 3 and 9, were synthesized. Both of these compounds did not form a covalent bond with the protein. In compound 9, two methyl groups located at the crucial α carbon replaced the proton that needed to be removed. In compound 3, the third methylene group prevented the β-elimination reaction. Furthermore, the concept of formation of vinylsulfone fragment was demonstrated by synthesizing compound 15 bearing the vinylsulfone itself. This compound readily formed the covalent bond with proteins. Since it appeared that compounds bearing ester groups (e.g. compounds 17 and 20) may have too high rate of covalent bond formation leading to non-desired modification of non-targeted proteins, we have designed and synthesized compounds bearing the carbamate functional group (e.g. compounds 18 and 22). The carbamate group was more stable than the ester and thus the covalent modification reaction of the protein showed milder rate than the ester. The cyclooctyl or cyclododecyl rings present in covalent compounds 20–24 and in non-covalent compounds 10–11 have been previously designed by our group to specifically bind to CAIX isozyme and intended not to bind to the other eleven human catalytically active CA isozymes. The ring could fit to the pocket in CAIX, but not so readily to other isozymes (Dudutienė et al., 2014; Zubrienė et al., 2017). The three-way recognition model is shown in Figure 3. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101401/elife-101401-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** First, the negatively charged sulfonamide forms a coordination bond with the Zn(II). Second, the hydrophobic cyclooctyl ring fits into the hydrophobic pocket of the CAIX isozyme and provides substantial selectivity over other CA isozymes. Third, a covalent bond forms with the histidine providing irreversible inhibition of CAIX enzymatic activity. ### Covalent interaction between inhibitors and CA isozymes by X-ray crystallography The covalent bond between the compounds and protein was demonstrated by X-ray crystallography (Figure 4). The crystal structures of compounds 21, 20, and 23 with CAI, CAII, and CAIX, respectively, showed covalent bond formation between the ligands and the histidine residue of the enzymes. In CAI, the ligand forms a covalent bond with His 67, while in CAII and CAIX, the bond is made with His 64 – a residue responsible for proton shuttle function in CA isoforms (Fisher et al., 2005). The distance between the nitrogen atom of histidine and the vinyl carbon atom of the compounds was around 1.5 Å, consistent with the length of the covalent bond, and was visible with strong electron density in all three crystal structures (Figure 4A, B and C). Electron density was overall good for the whole ligand in all three crystal structures, with slightly weaker electron density observed in the hydrophobic tail region indicating higher flexibility. The hydrophobic tail part is oriented towards the active site region, which varies most between CA isozymes (the so-called ‘hot spot’ for isozyme (isoform)-selective inhibitor design Alterio et al., 2009). There are two protein subunits in the CAI structure, the position of the modeled 21 is very similar in both. The electron density of the ligand is better in protein chain B. Sulfonamide group and modification of His67 with para-linker are visible. The fluorine atoms of the benzene ring also could be located clearly, but the electron density of the benzene ring is partially lost. This could be explained by partial occupancy of the modeled conformation of the inhibitor and by rotation of ligand fraction since the ligand is probably not fixed by the covalent bond with His67. The cyclooctyl group is visible in both subunits only partially due to the flexibility of the ring resulting in multiple conformations. This group is oriented towards the hydrophobic part of the active site, defined by Leu131, Ala135, Leu141, and Leu198. ### Covalent interaction by mass spectrometry and enzymatic activity The mass spectra of CA isoforms incubated with compound 12 showed a 319 Da shift compared to pure CA isoforms (except CAIII), equal to compound 12 molar mass without the ester group (Table 2). Moreover, after a 3-min incubation of 1:1 molar ratio of compound 12 with CAXIII protein (29,575 Da), nearly half of the protein was already covalently modified in this time as shown by an additional 29,894 Da peak (319 Da shift, Figure 5A). After 2 hr of incubation, essentially entire protein fraction was covalently modified by the compound. The presence of the minor peak at 30,213 Da (638 Da shift) in Figure 5A indicates that there is a second modification site on CAXIII protein. _*CA IX mutant C174S, N346Q, prepared in yeast as described in Leitans et al., 2015._ The peptide mapping by digestion of the CAXIII with thrombin detected the compound 12 covalently bound exclusively to the peptide containing His64 residue (Figure 5—figure supplements 21 and 22). However, in the 1H-15N-HSQC 2D NMR spectrum, upon incubation of CAII isozyme at 1:1 molar ratio for 1 hr with covalent compound 12, in addition to the His64 signal change, we observed a decrease of peak intensity in the N-terminal part of CAII indicating an additional minor fraction of enzyme with covalently bound 12 outside CA active site (Figure 5—figure supplements 23 and 24). Thus, ester compound 12 may be too reactive for fully specific inhibition. The non-covalent compound 6 was incubated with CAII at a tenfold surplus of the compound, but no covalent modification was detected (Figure 5—figure supplement 16). Therefore, a series of compounds bearing the carbamate leaving group were designed (18, 19, and 22) to reduce chemical reactivity and reduce undesired reactions with non-intended groups. Compound 22 exhibited covalent modification of CAIX, but after 4 hr incubation, there was still a significant part of non-modified protein present. Thus the reaction was significantly slower than with the ester group. The MW of CAIX as calculated from the sequence was 28061.68 Da and matched closely the measured mass of 28060.32 (Figure 5B top panel and Figure 5—figure supplement 20) or 28060.45 (lower panel). The calculated MW of compound 22 was 563.1372 Da and was measured to be 564.1444 Da. The calculated mass of compound 22 without the carbamate leaving group was 426.0895 Da, while the measured difference in Figure 5B was 426.41 Da, a perfect match. Thus, compound 22 exhibited both highly specific and relatively slow modification of CAIX, with a good perspective toward drug design. The covalent irreversible and non-covalent reversible interaction was also demonstrated by comparing the inhibition of enzymatic activity of CAIX by non-covalent compound 5 and covalent compound 20 and their possibility to be dialyzed out. Both compounds fully inhibited the enzymatic activity of CAIX at 1:1 molar ratio in the same dose-dependent manner. The resultant protein-ligand complex was then subjected to 32 hr dialysis. The CAIX complex with the non-covalent 5 regained 73% of the original enzymatic activity, while the CAIX with covalent 20 did not regain any detectable enzymatic activity (Figure 5C and D). This indicates that the covalent modification irreversibly inhibited the enzymatic activity of CAIX. To determine the contribution of the primary sulfonamide group on the capability of making a covalent bond with CA, we synthesized a secondary sulfonamide 13 and compared it with the analogous covalent compound 12. After 2 hr of incubation at 10:1 molar surplus of secondary sulfonamide 13, the free CAII protein still dominated, indicating that only a minor fraction of the protein was covalently modified (Figure 5—figure supplement 17B). In comparison, using the same conditions, compound 12 bearing the primary sulfonamide group completely modified CAII (Figure 5—figure supplement 17C). This shows the significant effect of the primary sulfonamide group in guiding the compound into the CA active site and consequent covalent bond formation with His64 amino acid. In the absence of the guiding sulfonamide group, such as in 13, a relatively slow modification most likely occurred on nucleophilic residues different than the His64 in the protein active site. This unintended covalent modification by the secondary-sulfonamide 13 was also observed with isozymes other than CAII. Although this compound should have low affinity to all CA isozymes, it still modified CAXIII at a 10:1 compound surplus molar ratio after 2 hr incubation (Figure 5—figure supplement 18). This inhibition mode may occur in two stages. In the first stage, the inhibitor interacts with the enzyme due to its affinity to the targeted enzyme. Here, the affinity is determined by the primary sulfonamide group and the hydrophobic substituent in the meta position. The compound is still able to reversibly dissociate and its non-covalent binding affinity is quantified by the dissociation constant Kd, defined as the ratio of dissociation and association rate constants koff/kon: $$ E+I⇌k_{off}k_{on}E⋅I→k_{trans}E⋅A→k_{inact}E−A $$ In the second stage, the pre-vinylsulfone compound is chemically transformed into the reactive vinylsulfone electrophile by a basic amino acid of the enzyme at a rate of ktrans. In the final reaction step, the vinylsulfone may form a covalent bond with the nucleophilic residue with a specific inactivation rate constant kinact. Since the vinylsulfone is highly reactive, ktrans must be rate-limiting and accounting for the apparent inactivation rate, much slower than for vinyl sulfone 15. It is incorrect to state covalent compound affinities in terms of a conventional dissociation constant Kd. Therefore, the apparent dissociation constant is valid only to a limited extent because if there is an irreversible chemical modification, then eventually all of the protein will be modified independent of the affinity. In our case, we can assume a rapid pre-equilibrium followed by a slow covalent modification. Therefore, relative affinity measurements are valid both by competition assay described above and the fluorescence-based thermal shift assay, described below. However, due to the interplay of kinetic and thermodynamic equilibrium contributions, the affinity measurements should still be considered with caution. We applied the fluorescence-based thermal shift assay to determine the apparent dissociation constants Kd,app of covalent compounds to arrange them in the order of their apparent affinities (association rate constants). The designed group of compounds bound to CAIX, an anti-cancer target protein, via a triple binding model: (1) the sulfonamide group formed a coordination bond with the Zn(II) in the active site, (2) the hydrophobic ring selectively recognized CAIX over other CA isozymes, and (3) covalent bond formed between the compound and histidine residue of the protein. To reduce reactivity, compounds with the carbamate leaving group were designed. A large series of synthesized compounds distinguish the chemical structures necessary for covalent modification from non-covalent reversible interaction with the protein. In recent years, covalent inhibitors gained much attention due to their advantages such as complete target protein inhibition, low dosage, and effectiveness against mutated targets (unless mutation happens in the targeted nucleophilic residue; Lonsdale and Ward, 2018; Baillie, 2016; Kim et al., 2021). Although there is still a lot of concern for covalent compounds' off-target toxic effects, success stories like ibrutinib or, almost a century ago discovered penicillin and aspirin prove that carefully designed covalent compounds can be safely used (Byrd et al., 2014; Singh et al., 2011). To this day, the most used strategy in the design of covalent inhibitors is by attaching an optimized ‘warhead’ to a known lead compound. Such inhibitors exhibit efficient and full target inactivation. Quite a few known electrophilic groups are acting as efficient covalently modifying warheads. However, it is necessary to choose electrophiles with balanced reactivity to avoid off-target toxicity while maintaining steady covalent bond formation with targeted amino acid residue. Thus, among many discovered warheads only six are FDA-approved (De Vita, 2021). To the best of our knowledge, the fragment SO2CH2CH2OCOR has never been previously described in the literature as a precursor of warhead, a pro-drug capable of rearranging to vinyl-sulfonyl moiety and forming a covalent bond with the target enzyme. Nevertheless, it is known that compounds bearing SO2CH2CH2OCOR fragments can rearrange to vinyl-sulfonyl moiety which has been known as a covalently modifying warhead by reacting with lysine/cysteine residues (De Vita, 2021). In most cases, it was demonstrated by chemical reactions in basic environments (Tsutsui et al., 1987; Alonso et al., 2003; Ichikawa et al., 1989). However, here we demonstrate that the vinyl-sulfonyl group can react with the His residue. Formation of the covalent bond was shown by X-ray crystallography and 2D NMR. The inability to regain enzymatic activity by dialysis of the compound also confirmed the covalent bond formation. Several methods exist for comparing the affinity of covalent inhibitors for a target protein, such as comparing compound Kd, IC50, or Ki (Lonsdale and Ward, 2018; Ruddraraju and Zhang, 2017). However, due to the time-dependent nature of covalent inhibitor action, the conventional comparisons become challenging or even impractical using these parameters (Lonsdale and Ward, 2018; Ruddraraju and Zhang, 2017). In the case of IC50, this value represents the compound concentration inhibiting half of the target enzyme molecules. However, in the case of covalent inhibitors that react irreversibly but slowly, given enough time, covalent inhibitors should give IC50 values equal to half of the target concentration as a result of disrupted binding equilibrium (Strelow, 2017). The same principle applies to Ki, where if covalent bond formation outpaces compound dissociation, leading to near zero koff, the observed Ki values should also approach zero over time. Thus, the Ki alone is insufficient, since it does not take into account the second stage involving covalent bond formation. In a covalent inhibition model, where initial non-covalent binding precedes covalent bond formation, the most accepted way of describing covalent inhibitor binding commonly involves using kinact/Ki or % covalent occupancy derived from covalent kinetics and pharmacokinetics (Strelow, 2017). This approach, however, has limitations, especially with compounds exhibiting extremely high picomolar apparent affinities. We propose and have demonstrated that the thermal shift assay could be employed for the precise determination of such affinities. Considering the already complicated covalent inhibitor evaluation due to two-step mechanism, it is even harder to assess compounds bearing SO2CH2CH2OCOR fragments because they act as prodrugs. We must consider an additional step – the elimination reaction, during which an active compound is formed, capable of binding to the protein covalently. Without the elimination step, the active compound is not formed, and the formation of a covalent bond with CA is impossible. If the elimination reaction rate is higher than the covalent bond formation rate, we can ignore it and consider it as part of kinact because the limiting step will be kinact. However, it is challenging to determine separate and correct Ki, elimination rate constant, and kinact values for CA isozymes because of exceptionally high compound affinity. Nevertheless, using fluorescent thermal shift assay (FTSA), we could determine the Kd,app for all 12 catalytically active CA isozymes and could perform an affinity correlation between different CA isozymes. Prior applications of the thermal shift were limited to testing the change in the melting temperature of the protein upon covalent modification (Udompholkul et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021; Iliev et al., 2022; Qiao et al., 2023; Gambini et al., 2019). Therefore, to the best of our knowledge, the apparent affinity determination by FTSA of covalent compound binding to proteins is being demonstrated here for the first time. There are only a few examples of covalent inhibitors of CA – bromoacetazolamide and N-bromoacetylacetazolamide and several compounds designed for enzyme tagging which have been tested on CAII as a model enzyme (Kandel et al., 1970; Chen et al., 2003; Takaoka et al., 2006). In bromoacetazolamide case, even with 20 molar surpluses, bovine CAII was not fully modified even after 24 hr (Takaoka et al., 2006). The experiments with bromoacetazolamide were performed in the basic environment (pH 8.2 and 8.7), which was a favorable condition for covalent bond formation and thus it is hard to compare with other compounds (Kandel et al., 1968). The covalent tag-bearing vinyl-sulfonyl warhead showed better results compared to bromoacetazolamide (>90% of compound covalently bound to bovine CAII after 10 hr at pH 7.4). The compounds 20 and 12 irreversibly bound and inhibited most of the human CA isoforms in less than 2 hr (at pH 7.0) and possibly are the first covalent CA inhibitors tested against CA isozymes, except the above-described inhibitors of CAII and CAI, with vinyl-sulfonyl reacting with the histidine residue (Chen et al., 2003). To assess the potential of covalent compounds for drug development, it is crucial to investigate whether they can indiscriminately react with different histidine and nucleophilic groups in proteins. Our testing involved examining the binding of these compounds to live cancer cells, thereby interacting with all proteins exposed on the cancer cell surface. The results demonstrated that these compounds exhibited specific and exclusive binding to the target protein CAIX, expressed in hypoxia-grown cancer cells. Notably, these compounds displayed the highest affinities among numerous CAIX inhibitors described in the literature, and their covalent binding led to irreversible inactivation of CAIX expressed in live cancer cells. This compelling evidence suggests significant potential for the development of these compounds as anticancer drugs. ## Materials and methods ### Enzyme purification All recombinant human CA isozymes were produced as described previously by using either bacterial or mammalian expression system (Dudutienė et al., 2014; Mickevičiūtė et al., 2019). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.101401.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101401.3.sa2)

Summary:

The authors utilized a "ligand-first" targeted covalent inhibition approach to design potent inhibitors of carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX) based on a known non-covalent primary sulfonamide scaffold. The novelty of their approach lies in their use of a protected pre-vinylsulfone as a precursor to the common vinylsulfone covalent warhead to target a nonstandard His residue in the active site of CAIX. In addition to biochemical assessment of their inhibitors, they showed that their compounds compete with a known probe on the surface of HeLa cells.

Strengths:

The authors use a protected warhead for what would typically be considered an "especially hot" or even "undevelopable" vinylsulfone electrophile. This would be the first report of doing so making it a novel targeted covalent inhibition approach specifically with vinylsulfones.

The authors used a number of orthogonal biochemical and biophysical methods including intact MS, 2D NMR, x-ray crystallography, and an enzymatic stopped-flow setup to confirm the covalency of their compounds and even demonstrate that this novel pre-vinylsulfone is activated in the presence of CAIX. In addition, they included a number of compelling analogs of their inhibitors as negative controls that address hypotheses specific to the mechanism of activation and inhibition.

The authors employed an assay that allows them to assess target engagement of their compounds with the target on the surface of cells and a fluorescent probe which is generally a critical tool to be used in tandem with phenotypic cellular assays.

Weaknesses:

This reviewer does not find any major weaknesses beyond those noted in the first round of review.

I understand that some of the previously suggested experiments are cumbersome and I look forward to seeing this manuscript published as well as follow-up on this work in the future.

Summary:

Targeted covalent inhibition of therapeutically relevant proteins is an attractive approach in drug development. This manuscript now reports a series of covalent inhibitors for human carbonic anhydrase (CA) isozymes (CAI, CAII, and CAIX, CAXIII) for irreversible binding to a critical histidine amino acid in the active site pocket. results.result: The authors designed and synthesized novel pre-vinylsulfone prodrug compounds containing: (1) a primary sulfonamide group for CA recognition, (2) high-affinity moieties (cyclooctyl/cyclododecyl rings) for CAIX selectivity, and (3) SO2CH2CH2OCOR groups (esters or carbamates) that transform into reactive vinylsulfone warheads capable of covalently modifying His64 in the active site. This represents a novel warhead strategy for targeted covalent inhibition of histidine residues.
results.evaluation: The claims are well-supported by extensive synthetic chemistry data (C57, C64, C167), structural characterization, and mechanistic evidence. The three-way recognition model (C4-C6, C81, C166) is clearly articulated and supported by control compounds (C70-C73) that validate the mechanism. The novelty of the pre-vinylsulfone warhead for histidine modification is established (C16, C63, C176).

results.result: The covalent modification mechanism proceeds via β-elimination of the SO2CH2CH2OCOR group in the enzyme active site, facilitated by fluorine electron-withdrawal, to generate a reactive vinylsulfone that then forms a covalent bond with His64. This mechanism was validated through control compounds (3, 9, 15) and requires specific structural features including the SO2 group at the para position and the -O-CO-R leaving group.
results.evaluation: The proposed mechanism is well-supported by systematic structure-activity relationships (C67-C68), control compounds that prevent elimination (C70-C73), and demonstration that pre-formed vinylsulfone (compound 15) readily forms covalent bonds (C74-C75). The requirement for specific structural features is clearly demonstrated through negative controls. The novelty of applying this chemistry to enzyme inhibition is established (C63, C176).

results.result: X-ray crystallography confirmed covalent bond formation between the compounds and histidine residues in CA isozymes, with compounds 21, 20, and 23 forming covalent bonds with His67 in CAI and His64 in CAII and CAIX. The distance between the histidine nitrogen and vinyl carbon was ~1.5 Å, consistent with covalent bond length, with strong electron density visible in all structures.
results.evaluation: The crystallographic evidence (C82-C86) provides direct structural confirmation of covalent bond formation with appropriate bond distances and electron density. The data are presented with proper refinement statistics (Table 1) and multiple structures across different CA isozymes strengthen the conclusions. This represents gold-standard evidence for covalent modification.

results.result: Mass spectrometry confirmed covalent modification of CA isozymes by compound 12, showing a 319 Da mass shift (corresponding to compound minus ester group) for all isozymes except CAIII. Peptide mapping confirmed exclusive modification of the His64-containing peptide in CAXIII. However, NMR data revealed minor off-target modification in CAII, suggesting ester compound 12 may be too reactive for fully specific inhibition.
results.evaluation: The MS data (C87-C91, C98-C100) provide strong evidence for covalent modification with precise mass shifts matching the expected values. Peptide mapping (C91) confirms site-specificity for the primary modification site. The NMR evidence (C92) appropriately identifies a limitation (off-target modification), and the authors correctly conclude that ester 12 may be too reactive (C93, C101). The inclusion of negative control compound 6 (C94) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Carbamate-containing compounds (18, 19, 22) were designed as less reactive alternatives to ester compounds, showing significantly slower (at least 100-fold) covalent modification rates while maintaining specificity. Compound 22 exhibited highly specific but slower modification of CAIX, representing an optimized balance between reactivity and selectivity suitable for drug design.
results.evaluation: The design rationale (C76-C77, C95, C116) is clearly articulated and supported by comparative data showing slower reaction rates for carbamates versus esters (C78, C97, C117). The characterization of compound 22 (C96-C101) demonstrates the desired properties. The conclusion about achieving a good balance for drug design (C101, C157) is reasonable based on the presented data.

results.result: Dialysis experiments demonstrated irreversible inhibition by covalent compounds. Both non-covalent compound 5 and covalent compound 20 fully inhibited CAIX enzymatic activity at 1:1 molar ratio, but after 32-hour dialysis, CAIX with non-covalent 5 regained 73% activity while CAIX with covalent 20 showed no detectable activity recovery, confirming irreversible covalent modification.
results.evaluation: The dialysis experiment (C102-C107) is well-designed to distinguish reversible from irreversible inhibition. The comparison between covalent and non-covalent compounds provides appropriate controls, and the results clearly demonstrate irreversibility of covalent modification (C107, C181). The experimental design and interpretation are sound.

results.result: The primary sulfonamide group is essential for guiding compounds to the CA active site and enabling specific His64 modification. Secondary sulfonamide 13 showed minimal covalent modification of CAII (only minor fraction after 2 hr at 10:1 ratio) compared to complete modification by primary sulfonamide 12 under identical conditions, with modification by 13 likely occurring at different nucleophilic residues outside the active site.
results.evaluation: The comparison between primary (12) and secondary (13) sulfonamides (C108-C115) provides strong evidence for the importance of the primary sulfonamide in directing site-specific modification. The MS data clearly show the difference in modification efficiency (C109-C110), and the inference about off-target modification by 13 (C112, C115) is reasonable given its low affinity for CA isozymes.

results.result: Covalent compounds specifically bound to CAIX expressed on live HeLa cell surfaces in a dose-dependent manner, competing with fluorescein-labeled GZ19-32. Para-substituted non-selective compounds (12, 18) showed weaker binding (15-22 nM) than meta-substituted CAIX-selective compounds, with ester compounds 20 and 24 exhibiting single-digit nanomolar affinities (1.8-4.0 nM) and carbamate compound 22 showing the highest affinity (300 pM) for cell-surface CAIX.
results.evaluation: The cell-based competition assay (C119-C125) provides strong evidence for specific binding to CAIX on live cells without off-target modification of abundant cell-surface proteins. The systematic comparison of compounds with different structural features (C126-C135) demonstrates clear structure-activity relationships. The conclusion that compound 22 is a lead candidate (C136-C137) is well-supported by the data showing highest affinity and irreversible inhibition.

results.result: Fluorescence-based thermal shift assay (FTSA) was used to determine apparent dissociation constants (Kd,app) of covalent compounds across all 12 catalytically active CA isozymes. Compound 22 showed extremely tight binding to CAIX (Kd,app = 7.8 pM), representing the highest affinity among known CAIX-binding compounds. Covalent compounds showed 10-1000-fold higher apparent affinity than their non-covalent analogs, with the measurements being time-independent.
results.evaluation: The FTSA methodology (C147) is appropriate for comparing relative affinities of covalent compounds, and the time-independence validation (C150) addresses a key concern. The comprehensive dataset across all CA isozymes (C154) is valuable. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge limitations in interpreting Kd,app for covalent compounds (C142-C146), noting the interplay of kinetic and thermodynamic factors. The claim of highest affinity for CAIX (C148) is supported by the data presented.

results.result: The lead covalent CAIX-targeting compounds achieved picomolar affinities, with compound 22 reaching 7.8 pM (FTSA) or 2 pM (abstract claim), representing the highest affinity among known CAIX inhibitors and a rare level of affinity among any protein-ligand interactions.
results.evaluation: There is a discrepancy between the reported affinities: the abstract claims 2 pM (C9), while the FTSA data shows 7.8 pM for compound 22 (C148), and the cell-based assay shows 300 pM (C135). These differences may reflect different assay methods and the complex kinetics of covalent inhibitors, but the inconsistency should be clarified. The claim of "highest among known CAIX inhibitors" (C9, C148, C163) requires comparison with literature values not fully presented. The interpretation of apparent Kd for covalent compounds remains challenging as acknowledged by the authors (C142-C146).

results.result: The cyclooctyl or cyclododecyl ring at the meta-position provides CAIX selectivity by fitting into a hydrophobic pocket in CAIX but not readily into other isozymes. This structural feature both increases affinity for CAIX and greatly reduces affinity for non-target CAI and CAII, as part of a three-way recognition model involving sulfonamide-Zn coordination, selective ring recognition, and covalent His modification.
results.evaluation: The selectivity mechanism (C80-C81, C162) is supported by prior work from the same group (citations in C80) and consistent with the binding data showing differential affinities across isozymes (Table 4). The three-way recognition model (C81) integrates multiple lines of evidence including crystallography, binding data, and structure-activity relationships. The explanation is mechanistically sound and well-supported.

results.result: A dual CAIX/CAXII targeting strategy may be beneficial since both isozymes are overexpressed in some cancers, while inhibition of the remaining 10 CA isozymes would cause harm. The covalent bond provides several hundred-fold gain in affinity, and compound 22 is more promising than compound 23 as a drug candidate due to slower covalent bond formation rate and lower off-target toxicity risk.
results.evaluation: The rationale for dual CAIX/CAXII targeting (C158-C160) is reasonable based on cancer biology knowledge. The quantification of affinity gain from covalent bonding (C161) is supported by the comparative data in Table 4 and Figure 8. The preference for compound 22 over 23 (C164) is justified by the slower reaction kinetics of carbamates versus esters, reducing off-target modification risk. However, the claim about "harm" from inhibiting other isozymes (C160) is stated without supporting data.

results.result: Background on carbonic anhydrases and CAIX: There are 12 catalytically active CA isozymes in humans with different cellular localizations. CAIX is a hypoxia-inducible transmembrane protein overexpressed in hypoxic solid tumors that participates in cancer cell proliferation, metastasis, and interacts with transporters and adhesion proteins. Targeting CAIX is proposed to have therapeutic benefits, and isozyme-selective inhibitors would be more beneficial than current non-selective CA inhibitors.
results.evaluation: These claims (C2-C3, C25-C42) represent well-established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. The characterization of CA isozymes, their localization, and CAIX's role in cancer are supported by the cited references. This provides appropriate context for the study but does not represent novel findings from this work.

results.result: Background on targeted covalent inhibition: TCI compounds bear warheads (usually Michael acceptors) that initially bind reversibly then form irreversible covalent bonds with nucleophilic residues (mostly cysteine). This provides advantages including prolonged action, full target inactivation, lower dosages, and higher selectivity. However, histidine has weaker nucleophilicity than cysteine, and existing histidine-targeting compounds are highly reactive with poor selectivity.
results.evaluation: These claims (C11-C24) represent accurate background knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. The description of TCI mechanisms, advantages, FDA-approved examples, and challenges with histidine targeting provides essential context for understanding the novelty of the current work. The characterization of existing histidine-targeting methods and their limitations is accurate.

results.result: Background on prior CA covalent inhibitors: Previous covalent inhibitors for CAI and CAII (bromoacetazolamide, N-bromoacetylacetazolamide) formed covalent bonds with His67 (CAI) or His64 (CAII) but research was discontinued. Recent studies used CA as a model protein for fluorescent probes, with some compounds showing selective His64 modification. Different warheads including S(IV) fluoride have been applied to modify His64 and His3.
results.evaluation: These claims (C43-C51) accurately represent prior work on covalent CA inhibitors, appropriately cited from the literature. This historical context is important for establishing the novelty of the current approach, particularly the distinction that prior compounds were either discontinued or designed as probes rather than therapeutic inhibitors. The background is accurate and relevant.

results.result: Summary of key findings: MS and X-ray crystallography confirmed covalent binding to His64. The sulfonylethyl ester/carbamate acts as a prodrug, undergoing elimination in the active site to form reactive vinylsulfone that then covalently modifies His64. This mechanism has great potential for developing high-affinity isozyme-selective compounds that could become precursors of new-generation drugs.
results.evaluation: These claims (C54-C56, C179-C181) accurately summarize the key findings that are supported by the detailed experimental evidence presented in other claim groups. The characterization of the prodrug mechanism (C55) is supported by the mechanistic studies. The forward-looking statement about potential (C56) is reasonable speculation based on the demonstrated proof-of-concept, though it remains to be validated through further drug development studies.

results.result: Initial compound design and discovery: The benzenesulfonamide group coordinates with Zn(II), and fluorine atoms were included to lower sulfonamide pKa and strengthen interaction. Surprisingly, compounds containing the -SO2CH2CH2OCOR group exhibited extremely strong binding affinity and formed unexpected covalent bonds with the protein.
results.evaluation: These claims (C58-C61) describe the initial design rationale and serendipitous discovery of covalent modification. The design logic for including fluorines (C59) is chemically sound. The characterization of the discovery as "unexpected" (C61) is appropriate given that this represents a novel warhead strategy. The claims are supported by the subsequent detailed mechanistic and binding studies.

results.result: Considerations for interpreting covalent compound affinities: Covalent compounds form irreversible bonds through a two-stage mechanism involving initial reversible binding followed by covalent modification. It is incorrect to use conventional Kd for covalent compounds since eventually all protein will be modified regardless of affinity. A rapid pre-equilibrium followed by slow covalent modification can be assumed, making relative affinity measurements valid but requiring cautious interpretation due to kinetic and thermodynamic contributions.
results.evaluation: These claims (C138-C146) provide important methodological considerations for interpreting the binding data. The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitations of using conventional dissociation constants for covalent inhibitors (C142-C143) and explain why relative comparisons remain valid (C145). This transparent discussion of limitations strengthens rather than weakens the overall conclusions and demonstrates scientific rigor.

results.result: Discussion of covalent inhibitors in drug development: Covalent inhibitors have gained attention for advantages including complete target inhibition, low dosage, and effectiveness against mutated targets. Despite concerns about off-target toxicity, successful examples (ibrutinib, penicillin, aspirin) demonstrate that carefully designed covalent compounds can be safe. The most common strategy is attaching optimized warheads to known leads, but balanced reactivity is essential, with only six warheads currently FDA-approved.
results.evaluation: These discussion points (C169-C175) provide appropriate context from the literature about covalent inhibitors in drug development. The cited examples of successful covalent drugs (C170) are accurate, and the emphasis on balanced reactivity (C174) is relevant to the design strategy employed in this work. The statement about only six FDA-approved warheads (C175) provides important perspective on the significance of developing new warhead chemistries.

results.result: Broader applicability and potential: Targeted covalent compounds possess high initial affinity and selectivity followed by complete irreversible inactivation. The strategy could potentially be applied to any disease drug target protein bearing a His residue near the active site, with potential for developing new-generation drugs.
results.evaluation: The claim about broader applicability to any protein with His near the active site (C10) is speculative and not directly tested in this work. While the proof-of-concept with CA isozymes is strong, extending this to other protein targets would require: (1) demonstration that the elimination mechanism works in different active site environments, (2) evidence that sufficient selectivity can be achieved for other targets, and (3) validation that the approach works for proteins beyond the CA family. These remain important future directions rather than established results.

results.result: The authors introduce a novel pre-vinylsulfone warhead strategy for targeted covalent inhibition. The compounds contain a SO2CH2CH2OCOR fragment that acts as a prodrug, undergoing elimination in the CA active site to form a reactive vinylsulfone that covalently modifies histidine residues. This approach has not been previously applied to enzyme covalent inhibitors.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm the novelty of this approach. One reviewer states this is 'the first report' of using a protected warhead for vinylsulfone electrophiles, making it 'a novel targeted covalent inhibition approach.' Another reviewer emphasizes 'the use of a novel covalent pre-cursor molecule that undergoes beta-elimination to form the vinyl sulfone in situ' as a key strength. The editor notes the 'unique fragment as a protected covalent warhead' and its 'broad utility.'

results.result: The compounds form covalent bonds specifically with histidine residues (His64 in CAII and CAIX, His67 in CAI). This was demonstrated by X-ray crystallography showing bond distances of ~1.5 Å consistent with covalent bonds, and confirmed by 2D NMR spectroscopy.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently praise the structural evidence. One reviewer highlights 'co-crystal structures of CAI, CAII, and CAIX in the presence of three such inhibitors' and notes 'The supportive X-ray crystallography and MS data are significant strengths.' Another reviewer emphasizes the authors 'used a number of orthogonal biochemical and biophysical methods including intact MS, 2D NMR, x-ray crystallography' to confirm covalency. No concerns were raised about the crystallographic or NMR evidence.

results.result: The mechanism of covalent modification involves β-elimination where a basic amino acid removes a proton to form the vinylsulfone moiety, which then forms a covalent bond with histidine. This was validated by control compounds (3 and 9) that cannot undergo elimination and did not form covalent bonds, while compound 15 bearing vinylsulfone itself readily formed covalent bonds.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly commend the mechanistic validation. One reviewer notes the authors 'included a number of compelling analogs of their inhibitors as negative controls that address hypotheses specific to the mechanism of activation and inhibition.' Another reviewer praises 'Sufficient structure-activity relationships across a number of leaving groups' as a strength. The use of control compounds to validate the elimination mechanism is not questioned.

results.result: Mass spectrometry data showed covalent modification of CA isozymes by compound 12, with a 319 Da mass shift corresponding to the compound minus the ester group. Peptide mapping confirmed the compound bound exclusively to the peptide containing His64.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently cite MS data as strong supporting evidence. One reviewer states 'The supportive X-ray crystallography and MS data are significant strengths.' Another notes the authors 'used a number of orthogonal biochemical and biophysical methods including intact MS' to confirm covalency. The peptide mapping data identifying His64 as the exclusive modification site is not challenged.

results.result: Dialysis experiments demonstrated irreversible inhibition: CAIX inhibited by covalent compound 20 did not regain enzymatic activity after 32 hr dialysis, while CAIX with non-covalent compound 5 regained 73% activity, confirming the covalent modification irreversibly inhibits enzymatic activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the enzymatic data. One reviewer notes 'Mass spectrometry and enzymatic recovery assays validate these findings' as convincing. Another states 'the results and cellular activity data are convincing.' The dialysis experiment demonstrating irreversibility is not questioned and is implicitly accepted as part of the overall validation strategy.

results.result: The lead covalent inhibitors achieved extremely high apparent affinity for CAIX, with compound 22 reaching 7.8 pM by thermal shift assay and 300 pM in cell-based competition assays—the highest affinity among known CAIX inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the affinity measurements. One reviewer notes the authors 'designed a series of covalent inhibitors and carefully selected non-covalent counterparts to make their findings about the selectivity of covalent inhibitors for CA isozymes quite convincing.' The editor states 'The data convincingly support the main conclusions of the paper.' While reviewers acknowledge the complexity of interpreting covalent inhibitor affinities, they do not dispute the reported values or their significance.

results.result: Carbamate-based compounds (e.g., 18, 22) were designed to reduce reactivity compared to ester compounds. These showed significantly slower (at least 100-fold) covalent modification rates, providing better balance between CAIX binding and reduced off-target reactivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the structure-activity relationships. One reviewer highlights 'Sufficient structure-activity relationships across a number of leaving groups, as well as binding moieties that impact binding and dissociation constants' as a strength. Another notes the authors 'included a number of compelling analogs' addressing mechanism and inhibition. The strategic design of carbamates to reduce reactivity is implicitly accepted as part of the overall approach.

results.result: In HeLa cells expressing CAIX under hypoxia, covalent compounds competed with fluorescent probe GZ19-32 for CAIX binding in a dose-dependent manner. At low concentrations (~10 nM), compounds competed effectively, suggesting they did not bind non-specifically to other abundant cell-surface proteins.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the cellular data. One reviewer states 'the results and cellular activity data are convincing.' Another notes the authors 'showed that their compounds compete with a known probe on the surface of HeLa cells' and describes the cell-surface competition assay as 'generally a critical tool to be used in tandem with phenotypic cellular assays.' The specificity inference from competition at low concentrations is not challenged.

results.result: The compounds employ a triple recognition model: (1) sulfonamide coordination to Zn(II), (2) hydrophobic ring (cyclooctyl/cyclododecyl) selective for CAIX over other CA isozymes, and (3) covalent bond with His64. The cyclooctyl/cyclododecyl rings at the meta-position increased CAIX affinity while greatly reducing affinity for CAI and CAII.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm the selectivity strategy. One reviewer notes the authors 'designed a series of covalent inhibitors and carefully selected non-covalent counterparts to make their findings about the selectivity of covalent inhibitors for CA isozymes quite convincing.' Another highlights 'Sufficient structure-activity relationships across a number of leaving groups, as well as binding moieties that impact binding and dissociation constants.' The triple recognition model is not questioned.

results.result: Comparison of secondary sulfonamide 13 with primary sulfonamide 12 showed the primary sulfonamide is essential for guiding compounds into the CA active site: compound 13 showed minimal covalent modification of CAII at 10:1 molar ratio after 2 hr, while compound 12 completely modified CAII under the same conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the use of control compounds and SAR studies. One reviewer notes 'a number of compelling analogs of their inhibitors as negative controls that address hypotheses specific to the mechanism of activation and inhibition.' Another highlights 'Sufficient structure-activity relationships' as a strength. The comparison demonstrating the importance of the primary sulfonamide is implicitly accepted as part of the overall validation.

results.result: Structure-activity relationship studies showed the SO2 group at the para position is necessary for covalent bond formation (compounds 4 and 5 with SO or S groups did not form covalent bonds), and the -O-CO-R group is required (compounds 2, 10, 7, 8 with -NH-CO-R or -CO-O-R did not form covalent bonds).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly commend the SAR studies. One reviewer states 'Sufficient structure-activity relationships across a number of leaving groups, as well as binding moieties that impact binding and dissociation constants' is a strength. Another notes 'compelling analogs of their inhibitors as negative controls.' The specific structural requirements are not questioned and are accepted as part of the comprehensive SAR analysis.

results.result: NMR and MS data revealed some off-target modification: compound 12 showed decreased peak intensity in the N-terminal region of CAII indicating minor modification outside the active site, and secondary sulfonamide 13 modified CAXIII at non-His64 sites. Even carbamates showed some ability to form multiple covalent bonds, though at much lower levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations about off-target effects. One reviewer notes 'I understand that some of the previously suggested experiments are cumbersome' suggesting awareness of limitations but acceptance of the current data. The authors' transparent reporting of off-target modifications and their strategy to address this through carbamate design is implicitly accepted as appropriate.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that conventional dissociation constants (Kd) are not strictly appropriate for covalent inhibitors due to irreversible modification, but argue that relative affinity measurements by competition assay and thermal shift assay are valid for comparing compounds, though should be interpreted with caution due to kinetic and thermodynamic contributions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not dispute this methodological caveat. One reviewer notes the authors 'used a number of orthogonal biochemical and biophysical methods' without raising concerns about the interpretation of affinity data. The acknowledgment of limitations in affinity measurements for covalent inhibitors is standard in the field and the reviewers implicitly accept the authors' approach to relative comparisons.

results.result: The authors propose that this strategy could be applied to any disease target protein with a His residue near the active site, and that targeting CAIX (and potentially CAXII) could have therapeutic benefits for cancer by affecting pH regulation, metabolism, invasion, and metastasis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the broader significance. The editor states these findings are 'important due to the broad utility of the approach for covalent drug discovery applications and could have long-term impacts on related covalent targeting approaches.' One reviewer notes 'Their approach of targeted binding of the covalent inhibitors to histidine in CA isozyme may have broad utility for developing covalent inhibitors.' The therapeutic speculation is not challenged.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the novelty of the approach (C1, C16, C52, C63, C64, C165, C176). OpenEval emphasizes the three-way recognition model and synthetic chemistry data, while peer reviewers explicitly call this 'the first report' of using a protected warhead for vinylsulfone electrophiles. Both evaluations are aligned in affirming the novelty and mechanistic validation.

Both strongly support the crystallographic evidence (C82-C86, C180). OpenEval describes it as 'gold-standard evidence' with proper refinement statistics, while peer reviewers highlight 'co-crystal structures' and 'supportive X-ray crystallography' as significant strengths. Complete agreement on structural validation.

Both support the mechanistic validation through control compounds (C67-C75). OpenEval emphasizes systematic SAR and controls that prevent elimination, while peer reviewers praise 'compelling analogs as negative controls' and 'sufficient structure-activity relationships.' Both agree the mechanism is well-validated.

Both support the MS evidence for covalent modification (C87-C91). OpenEval highlights precise mass shifts and peptide mapping confirming site-specificity, while peer reviewers cite 'supportive MS data' and 'orthogonal biochemical methods including intact MS.' Both accept the MS data as strong evidence.

Both support the dialysis experiment demonstrating irreversibility (C102-C107). OpenEval describes it as 'well-designed' with appropriate controls, while peer reviewers note 'enzymatic recovery assays validate these findings.' Complete agreement on the irreversibility evidence.

OpenEval flags UNCERTAIN due to discrepancies in reported affinities (2 pM vs 7.8 pM vs 300 pM) across C9, C53, C135, C148, C163, while peer reviewers SUPPORT the affinity measurements without challenging the reported values. This represents a notable divergence: OpenEval identifies inconsistencies requiring clarification, while peer reviewers accept the data as convincing.
